rows.jp: 「おい、太一」
rows.en: “Hey, Taichi.”

ghs.en: Sakuraba: "Hoy, Taichi."
ghs.assessment: The ordinary attention-getter おい is 'hey' here. 'Hoy' is an uncommon nautical or archaic-sounding interjection unsupported by the source voice.
ghs.remedy: Hey

rows.jp: あれ、桜庭？
rows.en: Huh, Sakuraba?

ghs.en: Oh my, Sakuraba?
ghs.assessment: あれ marks mild surprise or recognition, equivalent here to 'huh?' The English gives Taichi the markedly genteel exclamation 'oh my.'
ghs.remedy: Huh, Sakuraba?

rows.jp: 「ほら、原稿だ」
rows.en: “Here. Your script.”

ghs.en: Sakuraba: "Here, it's the script."

rows.jp: 原稿、なんの？
rows.en: Script? For what?

ghs.en: A script, what might it be?

rows.jp: 「……ＤＪなんだろう？」
rows.en: “...You're the DJ, aren't you?”

ghs.en: Sakuraba: "...you're the DJ aren't you?'
ghs.assessment: The dialogue begins with a double quotation mark but closes with an apostrophe, leaving mismatched quotation marks.
ghs.remedy: aren't you?"

rows.jp: ＤＪ、俺が？
rows.en: DJ? Me?

ghs.en: DJ... me?

rows.jp: そうだった気もする。
rows.en: Come to think of it, maybe I was.

ghs.en: It felt like it was true.

rows.jp: 「先輩のＤＪ、ちょっと楽しみー」
rows.en: “I'm kind of looking forward to hearing you DJ.”

ghs.en: Miki: "I'm sorta looking forward to your DJ, Senpai!"
ghs.assessment: DJ is the role or activity Taichi will perform, not a possessed person or object. The English therefore requires a gerund or role construction.
ghs.remedy: looking forward to hearing you DJ

rows.jp: ちょっとかい。
rows.en: Only kind of?

ghs.en: What's that 'sorta'?

rows.jp: 「わたしは、先輩が恥かくところが楽しみです」
rows.en: “I'm looking forward to watching you embarrass yourself.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Me, I am looking forwards to Senpai shaming himself."
ghs.assessment: In the phrasal verb 'look forward to,' 'forward' is not pluralized.
ghs.remedy: looking forward to

rows.jp: 恥かき決定なのかよ。
rows.en: My humiliation's a done deal?

ghs.en: You just decided I'll shame myself!

rows.jp: 「原稿、どうだ」
rows.en: “How's the script?”

ghs.en: Sakuraba: "Howsit, that script."
ghs.assessment: Sakuraba asks how the script is. The English uses the unrelated colloquial greeting 'howsit' and leaves 'that script' as a detached afterthought.
ghs.remedy: How's the script?

rows.jp: 悪くない、のではないかと思う。
rows.en: I think it might not be bad.

ghs.en: Not bad, maybe, I think.

rows.jp: 内容は……よくわからない。読めてはいるのに、理解できない。
rows.en: As for what's in it... I don't really know. I can read the words, but I can't understand them.

ghs.en: Contents... I don't really get this. Read I can read, but I can't understand.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese contrast means that Taichi can read the words but cannot understand them. The English reproduces the Japanese topic-focus order in an unnatural inversion.
ghs.remedy: I can read it

rows.jp: 「ちょっと、何ぼんやりしてんの？　しゃんとしなさいよ」
rows.en: “Hey, why are you spacing out? Get it together.”

ghs.en: Touko: "Come on now, what're you being all slack-jawed for? Be dignified already!"
ghs.assessment: Touko asks why Taichi is spacing out and tells him to pull himself together. 'Slack-jawed' adds an open-mouthed appearance, while 'be dignified' changes alertness and composure into social dignity.
ghs.remedy: Why are you spacing out? Pull yourself together.

rows.jp: 冬子……。
rows.en: Touko...

ghs.en: Touko...

rows.jp: 「何なのその顔。気合い足りないんじゃない？」
rows.en: “What's with that face? Where's your fighting spirit?”

ghs.en: Touko: "What's that face for. Don't you got enough fighting spirit now?"
ghs.assessment: After auxiliary 'do,' the verb must appear in its base form: 'have,' not 'got.'
ghs.remedy: Don't you have

rows.jp: 「とかいって、ラブラブー」
rows.en: “Says the girl who's all lovey-dovey.”

ghs.en: Miki: "Or maybe it's lovey-looove!"

rows.jp: 「ラブラブー」
rows.en: “Lovey-dovey.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Lovey-looove."

rows.jp: 「今なにか言ったかしら一年生～」
rows.en: “Did you say something, first-years?”

ghs.en: Touko: "I wonder if you just said something, you first ye～ars!"
ghs.assessment: The Japanese addresses the first-year students collectively. The English requires the compound noun 'first-years'; inserting the prolonged-sound mark inside 'years' does not supply the missing construction.
ghs.remedy: you first-yeaars

rows.jp: 「言ってませーん！」
rows.en: “Not a thing!”

ghs.en: Miki: "Said nooothing!"

rows.jp: 「ラブラブなんて、言ってません」
rows.en: “We certainly didn't say lovey-dovey.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Have said nothing like 'lovey-love'."
ghs.assessment: The English finite clause omits its subject.
ghs.remedy: I said nothing

rows.jp: 「斬っちゃおうかしら？」
rows.en: “Maybe I should cut you down.”

ghs.en: Touko: "Should I just slay them, I wonder?"
ghs.assessment: Touko directly threatens the first-years she is addressing. The English switches the targets into third-person 'them,' as if she were discussing absent people.
ghs.remedy: Maybe I should cut you two down?

rows.jp: 「あはは、やば。先輩助けて、斬られる」
rows.en: “Ahaha, yikes. Taichi, help—she's going to cut me down!”

ghs.en: Miki: "Ahahah, this is bad. Senpai, help, we'll be slain!"

rows.jp: 「先輩なら助けてくださいよ」
rows.en: “You ought to help us, Kurosu.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "You can help us, Senpai so get on it!"
ghs.assessment: Kiri appeals to the obligation attached to Taichi's senior status: if he is their senpai, he should help. The English instead states mere ability.
ghs.remedy: If you're our senpai, then help us

rows.jp: おいおい……都合良いな。
rows.en: Oh, come on... How convenient.

ghs.en: My my... I'm so convenient, am I.
ghs.assessment: 都合が良い here means that the others are opportunistically treating Taichi as useful when it suits them. The English instead calls Taichi himself convenient.
ghs.remedy: How convenient for you...

rows.jp: 「ちょっとどっちの味方なの、太一？」
rows.en: “Hey, whose side are you on, Taichi?”

ghs.en: Touko: "Really, Taichi, who are you allied with now?"

rows.jp: 「よっし、あった！　はぁ、あぶなかった……」
rows.en: “All right, found it! Whew, that was close...”

ghs.en: Tomoki: "The-ere, done! Sigh, that was close..."
ghs.assessment: Tomoki exclaims that he found the fault or connection he was seeking. 'Done' skips the discovery and presents the repair as already completed.
ghs.remedy: There, found it!

rows.jp: 「原因なんだったんだ？　接触不良か？」
rows.en: “What caused it? A bad connection?”

ghs.en: Sakuraba: "What caused that? Inadequate contact?"

rows.jp: 「いや、断線。だからケーブル類、買い直せって言ったんだけど」
rows.en: “No, a broken wire. That's why I said we should replace the cables.”

ghs.en: Tomoki: "Nope, severance. And that's why I toldja to go buy a better type of cable."
ghs.assessment: Tomoki says that a wire is broken and that he had told them to replace the cables. 'Severance' is not the normal term for this electrical fault, and the English invents a recommendation to buy a superior cable type.
ghs.remedy: No, a broken wire. That's why I told you to replace the cables.

highlights.text: go buy a better type of cable

rows.jp: 「そんなことしたら、みんなの焼肉代がなくなります」
rows.en: “If we do that, there won't be any money left for everyone's barbecue.”

ghs.en: Misato: "But if we had done that, there would not have been enough to cover the cost of yakiniku for everyone."

rows.jp: 「どっち優先してんだよ、姉さんは」
rows.en: “Which one comes first, Sis?”

ghs.en: Tomoki: "What're even your priorities, nee-san!"

rows.jp: はは、姉さん？
rows.en: Hah. Sis?

ghs.en: Hahah, 'nee-san'?

rows.jp: お姉ちゃんだろ？
rows.en: You mean Big Sis, right?

ghs.en: You mean 'onee-chan', right?

rows.jp: 「うるさいなぁ、自立の時なんだよ、ぼかぁ」
rows.en: “Oh, shut up. It's time I stood on my own, that's all.”

ghs.en: Tomoki: "Shaddap you, I'm at the time of self reliance, ah' am!"
ghs.assessment: Tomoki says that he has reached the age or stage of becoming independent. The English uses the calque 'at the time of,' omits the hyphen in 'self-reliance,' and invents a malformed eye-dialect tag.
ghs.remedy: I'm at the age when I need some independence!

highlights.text: I'm at the time of self reliance, ah' am!

rows.jp: あたたかい。
rows.en: Warm.

ghs.en: So warm.

rows.jp: あたたかい、世界だ。
rows.en: A warm world.

ghs.en: This world is so warm.

rows.jp: 「先輩、何もできませんけど、応援してます」
rows.en: “Taichi, I can't do anything, but I'm rooting for you.”

ghs.en: Yusa: "Senpai, I can't do anything, but I will be cheering!"

rows.jp: 遊紗ちゃん。
rows.en: Yusa.

ghs.en: Yusa-chan.

rows.jp: 放送部だったんだっけ？
rows.en: Was she in the broadcasting club?

ghs.en: She was in the Broadcast Club, was she?

rows.jp: 「……太一、制服が乱れてる」
rows.en: “...Taichi, your uniform is disheveled.”

ghs.en: Youko: "...Taichi, your uniform is disheveled."

rows.jp: 「＝心の乱れでもある」
rows.en: “= disorder in your heart, too.”

ghs.en: Youko: "= the heart itself is disheveled."

rows.jp: 曜子ちゃん……。
rows.en: Yoko...

ghs.en: Youko-chan...

rows.jp: 「ほら、直してあげるわ。睦美さんに恥をかかせるわけにはいかないもの」
rows.en: “Here, I'll fix it for you. We can't have you embarrassing Mutsumi.”

ghs.en: Youko: "Here, I will adjust it for you, yes. Embarrassing Mutsumi-san is completely unacceptable."

rows.jp: なんか、懐かしい感じだ。
rows.en: Something about this feels nostalgic.

ghs.en: It felt sorta... nostalgic,

rows.jp: けど。
rows.en: But.

ghs.en: but,

rows.jp: 適度に、優しい。
rows.en: Gentle in moderation.

ghs.en: suitably... gentle.

rows.jp: 適度に、厳しい。
rows.en: Strict in moderation.

ghs.en: Suitably... rigorous.

rows.jp: 「無性に旅に出たくなった。行くか」
rows.en: “I've got a sudden urge to travel. Want to go?”

ghs.en: Sakuraba: "I want to asexcessively go on a journey. Wanna go?"
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that Sakuraba has been seized by an urge to travel. The English fuses an adverb into the nonexistent word 'asexcessively' and places it inside an ungrammatical infinitive construction.
ghs.remedy: I've got an irresistible urge to travel.

highlights.text: I want to asexcessively go on a journey.

rows.jp: 「行くな……」
rows.en: “Don't go...”

ghs.en: Tomoki: "Don'tcha go..."

rows.jp: 「いつも思うんですけど、旅行の資金とかどうしてるんですか？」
rows.en: “I've always wondered—how do you pay for all these trips?”

ghs.en: Miki: "I'm always thinking of doing that, but what do I do about the travel expenses?"
ghs.assessment: Miki says that she has always wondered how Sakuraba finances his trips. The English instead says that Miki continually considers traveling and asks how she herself should handle the expense.
ghs.remedy: I've always wondered: how do you pay for your trips?

highlights.text: I'm always thinking of doing that, but what do I do about the travel expenses?

rows.jp: 「あるだけでやりくりするのが敏腕トラベラー」
rows.en: “A savvy traveler makes do with whatever he's got.”

ghs.en: Sakuraba: "Managing with just what you have somehow is what makes a competent Traveler."
ghs.assessment: The Japanese uses an ordinary descriptive compound for a capable traveler. The English arbitrarily capitalizes the common noun as though it were a formal title.
ghs.remedy: capable traveler

rows.jp: 「月給３０００円の自分には想像がつかないですねー」
rows.en: “My monthly salary's 3,000 yen, so I can't even imagine.”

ghs.en: Miki: "With a monthly allowance of 3,000 yen that's just sooo beyond even imagination."
ghs.assessment: 月給 means monthly pay or salary. The English changes Miki's earnings into money given to her as an allowance.
ghs.remedy: monthly salary

rows.jp: 「だまされちゃ駄目よ。桜庭の家って甘々なんだから。あるだけってのでたぶん何十万とかよ」
rows.en: “Don't let him fool you. Sakuraba's family spoils him rotten. When he says whatever he's got, he probably means hundreds of thousands of yen.”

ghs.en: Touko: "Don't you let yourself be fooled now! Sakuraba's family's made of naive spoiling. His 'just what you have somehow' must run in the hundreds of thousands!"
ghs.assessment: Touko says that Sakuraba's family is extremely indulgent toward him. The English depicts the family as physically made of an abstract and oddly qualified substance called 'naive spoiling.'
ghs.remedy: Sakuraba's family spoils him rotten.

highlights.text: Sakuraba's family's made of naive spoiling.

rows.jp: 「ぎょえ」
rows.en: “Gyeh.”

ghs.en: Miki: "Gwyoh!"

rows.jp: 「何十万？」
rows.en: “Hundreds of thousands?”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Hundreds of thousands?"

rows.jp: 「桜庭君停学」
rows.en: “Sakuraba, suspended.”

ghs.en: Misato: "Suspension, Sakuraba-kun!"

rows.jp: 「なぜだ……」

ghs.en: Sakuraba: "What for..."

rows.jp: 「旅先でホテルに泊まっているうちは、まだまだね」
rows.en: “If you're still staying in hotels when you travel, you've got a long way to go.”

ghs.en: Touko: "As long as you overnight at hotels while traveling, you still have a long way to go, mister!"

rows.jp: 「あ、ぺけくん時間です、覚悟はいいですか？」
rows.en: “Oh, X, it's time. Are you prepared?”

ghs.en: Misato: "Ah, Peke-kun, it is time, are you sufficiently prepared?"

rows.jp: 「さー、初めてのＤＪ、鬼が出るか」
rows.en: “Here we go—his first time DJing. Will we get a demon...”

ghs.en: Miki: "Who knows, it's his first DJ, maybe some demon will appear."
ghs.assessment: 鬼が出るか蛇が出るか is a paired idiom for not knowing what may emerge or happen. The English treats its first half as a literal prediction of a demon and does not communicate the idiom.
ghs.remedy: Who knows how his first time as DJ will turn out

rows.jp: 「蛇が出るか」
rows.en: “...or a snake?”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Maybe a snake will appear."
ghs.assessment: This is the answering half of 鬼が出るか蛇が出るか, a paired idiom meaning that the outcome is unknown. The English presents the snake as a literal possible event.
ghs.remedy: Could be anything.

rows.jp: 「悪い方しか想定されてないって」
rows.en: “You're only imagining bad outcomes.”

ghs.en: Tomoki: "Don't just assume something bad'll happen just because you never know what'll happen."
ghs.assessment: Tomoki objects that they are considering only bad outcomes. The English adds a causal explanation about general uncertainty that is not present in his retort.
ghs.remedy: You're only imagining bad outcomes.

highlights.text: just because you never know what'll happen

rows.jp: 「まー、がんばんなさい」
rows.en: “Well, do your best.”

ghs.en: Touko: "Well now, go do your best!"

rows.jp: 「頑張れよ」
rows.en: “Good luck.”

ghs.en: Sakuraba: "Do your best!"

rows.jp: 「楽しみですっ」
rows.en: “I can't wait!”

ghs.en: Yusa: "I look forwards to this!"
ghs.assessment: In the phrasal verb 'look forward to,' 'forward' is not pluralized.
ghs.remedy: look forward to

rows.jp: 「肩の力を抜いていきなさい」
rows.en: “Just relax and go for it.”

ghs.en: Youko: "Take the tension out of your shoulders now."
ghs.assessment: 肩の力を抜く is an idiom telling Taichi to relax and not try too hard. The English translates it as a literal physical extraction of tension from his shoulders.
ghs.remedy: Just relax and take it easy.

highlights.text: Take the tension out of your shoulders

rows.jp: ああ―――
rows.en: Yeah―――

ghs.en: Ahhh---

rows.jp: これはいい。
rows.en: This is nice.

ghs.en: This is just right.

rows.jp: 満たされる。
rows.en: I feel whole.

ghs.en: So fulfilling.

rows.jp: 都合の良さに、不安がよぎる。だけど。
rows.en: A flicker of unease passes through me at how convenient it all is. But.

ghs.en: In the convenience of this all, anxiety flashes by. However,
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that the suspicious convenience or perfection of the situation gives him a passing anxiety. The English uses a malformed prepositional phrase that does not identify what troubles him.
ghs.remedy: A flicker of anxiety passed through me at how convenient it all was.

highlights.text: In the convenience of this all

rows.jp: こんなに、幸せに感じられるじゃないか。
rows.en: I can feel this happy, can't I?

ghs.en: can't I just feel so much happiness now, with this?

rows.jp: なあ、みんな。
rows.en: Hey, everyone.

ghs.en: Well guys,

rows.jp: 馬鹿騒ぎを、しようぜ？
rows.en: Let's raise some hell, huh?

ghs.en: how about some horsing around?

rows.jp: そして目覚めると、もうすっかり昼になっていた。
rows.en: And when I wake, it's already the middle of the day.

ghs.en: And then I was awake, as it was already past noon.
Taichi: "Ngh..."

rows.jp: また学校に泊まってしまった。
rows.en: I ended up spending the night at school again.

ghs.en: I slept over at school again, dammit.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that he ended up sleeping at school again but contains no curse or explicit burst of anger.
ghs.remedy: I ended up sleeping at school again.

rows.jp: 人らしい日々のため、自宅に戻りたいところなのにな。
rows.en: I'd like to go home, if only for some semblance of a normal life.

ghs.en: When I have to go back to my house in order to live my days like a decent person...
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that he wants to return home in order to live something resembling ordinary human days. 'Decent person' introduces a moral judgment about his character.
ghs.remedy: to live something resembling a normal human life

rows.jp: でも一人で準備をするのは、なかなか大変だ。
rows.en: But getting everything ready alone is no easy task.

ghs.en: But getting this thing ready on my own is really really difficult.
ghs.assessment: なかなか means considerably or rather difficult. The English invents emphatic repetition unsupported by the source cadence.
ghs.remedy: really difficult

rows.jp: 先輩は偉かった。
rows.en: My predecessor was amazing.

ghs.en: Senpai was so admirable.

rows.jp: 「さーてと、今日もやるか」
rows.en: “All right, then. Let's get to it again today.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Sooo then now, shall we get down to it today as well?"

rows.jp: 意識的に声を出す。
rows.en: I make a conscious effort to speak aloud.

ghs.en: I deliberately vocalize.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi consciously speaks aloud. 'Vocalize' is a technical and intransitive description that obscures the simple act of using his voice.
ghs.remedy: I deliberately speak aloud.

rows.jp: そうしなければ、言葉を忘れてしまいそうで。
rows.en: Otherwise, I feel as though I might forget language.

ghs.en: It feels that if I don't do that, I could forget words themselves.

rows.jp: 作業開始。
rows.en: Work begins.

ghs.en: Beginning work.

rows.jp: 作業中止。
rows.en: Work stops.

ghs.en: Suspending work.

rows.jp: 「空腹」
rows.en: “Hungry.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Hunger."

rows.jp: 曜子ちゃんが作ってくれた弁当も、もはやない。
rows.en: Even the lunch Yoko made me is long gone.

ghs.en: The lunch that Youko-chan used to prepare was now also no more.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that the lunches once prepared for him are gone. The English reproduces the Japanese adverbial sequence in a nonidiomatic predicate.
ghs.remedy: was gone now too

rows.jp: 全て自分で用意だ。
rows.en: I have to prepare everything myself.

ghs.en: I have to arrange for everything myself.

rows.jp: 校内にはあのまずいカレーパン以外にも、コロッケパンがある。
rows.en: Besides that awful curry bread, the school also has croquette sandwiches.

ghs.en: Inside the school there is, in addition to that disgusting curry bread, some croquette bread.

rows.jp: 街にまで行けば、まあいろいろ食べられるだろう。
rows.en: If I go all the way into town, I can probably find any number of things to eat.

ghs.en: If I go out into town, well, I guess there's all sorts of stuff I could eat.

rows.jp: 周囲を見渡す。
rows.en: I look around.

ghs.en: I pass my gaze on the surroundings.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese simply says that Taichi looks around. The English calques the movement of a gaze into a malformed action performed 'on' the surroundings.
ghs.remedy: I look around.

highlights.text: I pass my gaze on the surroundings.

rows.jp: ……カレーパンの空袋が散らばっている。
rows.en: ...Empty curry-bread wrappers lie scattered everywhere.

ghs.en: ...empty packets of curry bread were scattered about.

rows.jp: うまいはずのコロッケパンも、口にする気にはならない。
rows.en: Even the croquette sandwiches—supposedly the good ones—don't tempt me.

ghs.en: I can't bring myself to even taste the croquette bread, however delicious it should be.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that even the croquette bread, which ought to taste good, fails to appeal to him. The English turns expected tastiness into an open-ended concessive degree and disconnects it from the speaker's prior knowledge.
ghs.remedy: even though it was supposed to be good

rows.jp: 静かな廊下。
rows.en: Quiet hallways.

ghs.en: Silent corridors.

rows.jp: 静かな部活。
rows.en: A quiet club.

ghs.en: Silent club activities.

rows.jp: 静かな日々。
rows.en: Quiet days.

ghs.en: Silent days.

rows.jp: 望んで得たもの。
rows.en: What I wanted, and what I got.

ghs.en: The obtainment of what I desired.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese noun phrase means 'what I wanted and obtained.' The English uses the awkward nominalization 'obtainment' and an unnecessary prepositional construction.
ghs.remedy: What I wanted and obtained.

highlights.text: The obtainment of what I desired.

rows.jp: 心は、楽。
rows.en: My mind is at ease.

ghs.en: The heart is at ease.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese refers to Taichi's own emotional state. The English turns his heart into a generic definite object detached from him.
ghs.remedy: My heart is at ease.

rows.jp: 誰も傷つけることのない世界。
rows.en: A world where no one gets hurt.

ghs.en: A world where the wounding of others cannot be.

rows.jp: 自分ができそこないって、自覚させられることのない世界。
rows.en: A world where no one makes me face what a failure I am.

ghs.en: A world where I am never made to be aware of how much of a good-for-nothing I am.

rows.jp: 改善しようのない素直な自分でいられる世界。
rows.en: A world where I can be my honest, unfixable self.

ghs.en: A world where I can live honestly about the impossibility of my ever improving.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that he can remain his unchangeably straightforward or unvarnished self. The English instead says that he honestly acknowledges a proposition about being unable to improve.
ghs.remedy: remain my unvarnished self, beyond any hope of improvement

highlights.text: live honestly about the impossibility of my ever improving

rows.jp: 素直な自分でいるということ。
rows.en: Being my honest self.

ghs.en: Living life in honesty with myself.

rows.jp: 仲間と青春しながら生きること。
rows.en: Living out my youth with friends.

ghs.en: Living the springtime of youth with close friends.

rows.jp: この二つはよくセットで用いられる概念なのに、俺の場合は破綻している。

rows.en: “...Still, if this were a real SOS, there would've been plenty of more efficient ways to do it.”

rows.jp: そして落ちた！
rows.en: And then it fell!

ghs.en: And then it fell!

rows.jp: 架空の枝を地面に引き寄せる力……引く力だ！
rows.en: The force that draws an imaginary branch down to the ground……a pulling force!

ghs.en: The power that draws the Air branch towards the ground... it's Pulling Power!
ghs.assessment: The Japanese calls the branch imaginary and then identifies the force drawing it toward the ground as an attractive force. The English changes 'imaginary' into 'Air' and invents a capitalized superhero-like name.
ghs.remedy: The force drawing the imaginary branch toward the ground... attraction!

rows.jp: フェンスは工業用の巨大ペンチみたいので破壊した。
rows.en: I destroyed the fence with something like an enormous pair of industrial pliers.

ghs.en: The fence was wrecked as if by a pair of gigantic industrial-use pliers.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi actually broke the fence with something like enormous industrial pliers. 'As if by' instead makes the pliers merely a visual comparison and removes the tool used.
ghs.remedy: with something like a gigantic pair of industrial pliers

highlights.text: as if by a pair of gigantic industrial-use pliers

rows.jp: 引力と名付けた！
rows.en: I named it gravity!

ghs.en: I shall name you Attractive Force... no, because this matter is most grave, Gravity!
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says only that he named the force 引力, attraction or gravity. The English invents a revision from one English name to another and adds an extended grave/gravity pun.
ghs.remedy: I named it gravity!

highlights.text: Attractive Force... no, because this matter is most grave, Gravity!

rows.jp: これは大発見だ。
rows.en: This is a tremendous discovery.

ghs.en: This is an important discovery.

rows.jp: 大航海時代のはじまりと終わり。
rows.en: The beginning and end of the Age of Discovery.

ghs.en: The beginning and the end of the Age of Discovery.

rows.jp: 切断したフェンス面が、不格好に滑空していく。
rows.en: The severed panel of fence glides away, ungainly.

ghs.en: The part of the fence that was cut down glides down awkwardly.

rows.jp: 無数の言葉。
rows.en: Countless words.

ghs.en: Words without number,

rows.jp: 脳を泳ぐ。
rows.en: Swimming through my brain.

ghs.en: swimming in the brain,

rows.jp: シナプス跳躍をして。
rows.en: Leaping from synapse to synapse.

ghs.en: taking the synaptic jump.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese depicts words leaping across synapses. The English turns the action into taking one definite object called 'the synaptic jump.'
ghs.remedy: leaping from synapse to synapse

rows.jp: ヤーヤー。
rows.en: Yah-yah.

ghs.en: Nooo, nooo.

rows.jp: 冬子が攻撃してきた。
rows.en: Touko attacked.

ghs.en: Touko came to attack,

rows.jp: 出会い別れそして再会という感動を挟む余地無し。
rows.en: No room to squeeze in the moving drama of meeting, parting, and reunion.

ghs.en: leaving no space for the interposing the deep emotions of meeting and parting and then reuniting.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that there is no room to insert the moving sequence of meeting, separation, and reunion. The English combines 'for' with the gerund's object in an ungrammatical construction.
ghs.remedy: no room to interpose the moving sequence

highlights.text: no space for the interposing the deep emotions

rows.jp: 母親も捜せないぜ。
rows.en: I cannot even search for my mother.

ghs.en: I can't locate Mother either.

rows.jp: 俺がしろしめしたいのは＊＊＊＊＊＊＊＊＊。
rows.en: What I wish to rule over is ＊＊＊＊＊＊＊＊＊.

ghs.en: What I wanna know is how to ru*********.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese completely censors the object after 'what I want to rule.' The English exposes an uncensored semantic lead-in inside the asterisks and therefore weakens the source's total redaction.
ghs.remedy: Censor the entire redacted expression after 'what I want.'

rows.jp: そして倒した。
rows.en: And then I defeated her.

ghs.en: And then she's defeated.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi then defeated her. The English removes him as agent and shifts the completed action into a present-state passive.
ghs.remedy: And then I defeated her.

rows.jp: すまん冬子！
rows.en: Sorry, Touko!

ghs.en: Sorry Touko!

rows.jp: じくり、と心が疼く。
rows.en: A slow throb of pain passes through my heart.

ghs.en: Squeak, and my heart aches like a living thing left out in the freezing winter.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese describes a slow, focused throb of pain in his heart. The English invents a squeaking sound and an elaborate image of a living creature abandoned in winter.
ghs.remedy: My heart throbbed with a slow ache.

highlights.text: like a living thing left out in the freezing winter

rows.jp: 血を感じた。
rows.en: I felt blood.

ghs.en: I felt blood.

rows.jp: 解放が必要だ。
rows.en: I need an outlet.

ghs.en: Liberation is necessary.

rows.jp: 自分で光らないと。
rows.en: I have to shine on my own.

ghs.en: I must shine by myself.

rows.jp: 汚名を挽回すべく、俺は霧を口説く。
rows.en: To recover my disgrace, I start wooing Kiri.

ghs.en: In order to redeem the stigma, I woo Kiri.

rows.jp: 名誉を返上すべく、ひたすら口説く。
rows.en: To relinquish my honor, I woo her relentlessly.

ghs.en: In order to relinquish the honor, I woo earnestly.

rows.jp: 口説き抜く。
rows.en: I woo her all the way through.

ghs.en: Woo continuously.
ghs.assessment: 口説き抜く means carrying the attempt through to the end and winning the person over, not merely wooing for an unspecified continuous duration.
ghs.remedy: I woo her to the bitter end.

rows.jp: 高らかに口説きあげる。
rows.en: I woo her at the top of my lungs.

ghs.en: Raising the loudness of the wooing.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that Taichi loudly or triumphantly talks Kiri up. The English turns the action into an abstract increase in the volume level of 'the wooing.'
ghs.remedy: I woo her at the top of my lungs.

highlights.text: Raising the loudness of the wooing.

rows.jp: 申し分のないナンパ。
rows.en: Flawless pickup artistry.

ghs.en: Uncriticizable Nanpa.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese calls it flawless pickup or flirting. 'Uncriticizable' is unnatural evaluative English, and leaving nanpa as a capitalized unexplained loanword obscures the action.
ghs.remedy: Flawless pickup artistry.

rows.jp: しかし色よい返事はもらえない。
rows.en: But I get no encouraging reply.

ghs.en: But a favorable response in good color I don't get.
ghs.assessment: 色よい返事 is an idiom for a favorable answer. The English translates the color component literally and follows Japanese word order into an ungrammatical inversion.
ghs.remedy: But I get no favorable answer.

highlights.text: a favorable response in good color I don't get

rows.jp: なぜか？
rows.en: Why?

ghs.en: How come?

rows.jp: それは霧が赤だからです。
rows.en: Because Kiri is red.

ghs.en: That would be because Kiri is scarlet.

rows.jp: 悔いる。
rows.en: I regret it.

ghs.en: Regret.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese is a finite action: Taichi regrets it. The English turns it into a bare abstract noun.
ghs.remedy: I regret it.

rows.jp: 畜生、畜生！
rows.en: Damn it, damn it!

ghs.en: Fuck, fuck!
ghs.assessment: 畜生 is a frustrated 'damn it' here. The English escalates the exclamation to the strongest ordinary English profanity without additional source support.
ghs.remedy: Damn it, damn it!

rows.jp: やらずに後悔するより、やって後悔すべきなのに！
rows.en: Even though you are supposed to regret doing it rather than regret never trying!

ghs.en: When it ought be better to regret doing than to regret not doing!
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that one should regret acting rather than regret never acting. The English begins with an ungoverned 'when' clause and omits 'to' after 'ought.'
ghs.remedy: I ought to regret doing it rather than regret not doing it!

rows.jp: 一人じゃ調整できないよ。
rows.en: I cannot calibrate myself alone.

ghs.en: I just can't get adjusted to being alone, you know.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that the required adjustment or coordination cannot be performed by one person alone. The English instead says that Taichi cannot psychologically acclimate to solitude.
ghs.remedy: I can't make the adjustment by myself.

rows.jp: さあ霧、オラの気持ちに応えてくれ！
rows.en: Come on, Kiri! Answer my feelings!

ghs.en: Well, Kiri, have a response to me's feelings!
ghs.assessment: The Japanese asks Kiri to respond to Taichi's feelings. The English uses 'me's' as an impossible possessive and the nonidiomatic collocation 'have a response to.'
ghs.remedy: answer my feelings

highlights.text: have a response to me's feelings

rows.jp: モノローグを駆使して俺は告った。
rows.en: Wielding my monologue, I confessed.

ghs.en: So I proclaimed while freely making use of monologue.
ghs.assessment: 告る is colloquial slang for confessing romantic feelings. 'Proclaimed' omits the romantic object and loses the slang distinction discussed immediately afterward.
ghs.remedy: I confessed my feelings

rows.jp: モノローグは独白って意味なんだけど、テレビゲーム文法における地の文というニュアンスで用いられるから重箱の隅とかつつきたい人はここを攻撃するといい。
rows.en: Monologue technically means soliloquy, but video game grammar uses it with the nuance of narration, so if you are the kind of person who likes to pick nits, this is a good place to attack.

ghs.en: Monologue has the meaning of speaking by oneself, however, with regards to videogame lingo, it is utilized in the nuance of descriptive and narrative text, so people who like to nitpick should start attacking that.

rows.jp: 実は告るって言葉嫌いだった。
rows.en: Actually, I have always hated “confess” as a verb.

ghs.en: Truth is, I hated the word 'proclaim'.
ghs.assessment: Taichi says that he dislikes the slang verb kokuru, 'confess one's love.' The English names a different ordinary English verb, breaking the metalinguistic link to the preceding line.
ghs.remedy: the word 'confess'

rows.jp: ハンパっぽいというか。
rows.en: It feels so half-baked.

ghs.en: It's sorta half-baked, should I say.

rows.jp: ギャランドゥがいい。
rows.en: Gyarandū is better.

ghs.en:
>   happy trail
Gyarandou is nice.
ghs.assessment: The English supplies a gloss but romanizes ギャランドゥ with an ad hoc ou ending. Standard Hepburn gives Gyarandū; if a documented Latin-script brand form is intended, that evidence must be recorded separately.
ghs.remedy: Gyarandū

rows.jp: うん、そうしよう。
rows.en: Yes. Let us do that.

ghs.en: Yeah, let's do that.

rows.jp: ではでは。
rows.en: Well then.

ghs.en: Then well then.

rows.jp: モノローグを駆使して俺はギャランドゥ。
rows.en: Wielding my monologue, I Gyarandū.

ghs.en: So I gyarandou'd while freely making use of monologue.
ghs.assessment: The improvised verb is built from a non-Hepburn romanization and then given an English apostrophe-d suffix. Standard Hepburn would retain the long vowel as Gyarandū before any functional wordplay solution.
ghs.remedy: Gyarandū'd

rows.jp: イカしてる。
rows.en: Stylish.

ghs.en: Daaaymn I'm so awesome.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that the newly coined expression is cool. The English makes Taichi praise himself personally, adds a curse, and greatly expands the line.
ghs.remedy: That's cool.

rows.jp: ギャラクシーって銀河っぽい単語と語感が似てるのもいい。
rows.en: I also like how Gyarandū and galaxy have a similar ring.

ghs.en: I like how it resembles the impact of the galaxy-like word Gyarak'shi too.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that Gyarandū has a pleasant phonetic resemblance to gyarakushī, 'galaxy.' The English changes sound into impact and supplies a malformed pseudo-romanization rather than standard Hepburn.
ghs.remedy: I also like how Gyarandū sounds a little like gyarakushī, 'galaxy.'

rows.jp: 似てねぇゆ。
rows.en: Does not sound a thing like it, yu.

ghs.en: No, 8, it resemblen't!

rows.jp: ゆ。
rows.en: Yu.

ghs.en:
Yu.
8

rows.jp: どっちかと言うと『ゆ』。
rows.en: If anything, it is closer to “yu.”

ghs.en:
If yu ask which, I'll tell yu it's "yu".
8

rows.jp: 『の』よりな。
rows.en: Than “no,” at least.

ghs.en: Better than that spiraly thing that's the >K<ana 'no'.

rows.jp: で、霧、どうなの？
rows.en: So, Kiri. What do you say?

ghs.en: So, Kiri, how about, 'K?
ghs.assessment: Taichi simply asks Kiri what she thinks. The English appends an unexplained apostrophe-K fragment that is absent from the Japanese wordplay sequence.
ghs.remedy: So, Kiri, what do you think?

rows.jp: 霧は真剣に言った。
rows.en: Kiri answered gravely.

ghs.en: Kiri said with an edge that wasn't of a wooden sword:
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says only that Kiri spoke seriously. The English invents an elaborate sword-edge contrast unrelated to the line.
ghs.remedy: Kiri answered seriously:

highlights.text: with an edge that wasn't of a wooden sword

rows.jp: 「……フライドチキンの性別が気になりますか？」
rows.en: “Do you care about the sex of your fried chicken?”

ghs.en: Kiri: "...are you worried about the gender of fried chicken?"

rows.jp: あー、なる、なるってそれ！
rows.en: Oh, I do! I absolutely do!

ghs.en: Ahhh, I am, I very much am!

rows.jp: じゃあ仕様がない。
rows.en: Then it can't be helped.

ghs.en: Well, it can't be specced.

rows.jp: 手榴弾が爆発しました。
rows.en: A hand grenade exploded.

ghs.en: The flashbang had exploded.
ghs.assessment: 手榴弾 is a hand grenade. A flashbang is a distinct non-fragmentation stun device.
ghs.remedy: hand grenade

rows.jp: 俺たちは死んだ。
rows.en: We died.

ghs.en: We had died.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese simple past states that the two died as the immediate result. The English past perfect incorrectly places that death before another past reference point.
ghs.remedy: We died.

rows.jp: あなたは武器を手によく戦ったが、蠍(さそり)の数は多く、突き立てられる毒針の全てを防ぐことは不可能だ。
rows.en: You fought well, weapon in hand, but the scorpions were many, and it was impossible to fend off every venomous stinger they drove at you.

ghs.en: With great armed skill you fought and well, but the scorpions were so many in number that defending from the stabbing of all their poisonous stingers was impossible.

rows.jp: やがて意識が薄らぎ、倒れると、蠍たちは久方ぶりのうまい人肉に歓喜しつつあなたの体を埋め尽くした。あなたの冒険は終わった。
rows.en: As your consciousness faded and you collapsed, the scorpions covered your body, rejoicing in their first taste of succulent human flesh in ages. Your adventure was over.

rows.jp: ウォーロック・モーロックの邪悪な計画を阻止するには、パラグラフの１に戻って冒険をやり直さなければならない。あなたの次なる冒険に、女神のじゅうぶんな加護があらんことを―――
rows.en: To thwart Warlock Morlock's evil scheme, you must return to paragraph 1 and begin your adventure again. May the Goddess richly bless your next adventure―――

ghs.en: To foil the evil plan of the Warlock Morlock, you must return to Paragraph 1 and redo your adventure from the beginning.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese continues with a full conventional benediction wishing the reader ample protection from the goddess on the next adventure. The English omits that entire closing sentence.
ghs.remedy: Add the omitted closing wish for the next adventure.

highlights.text: To foil the evil plan of the Warlock Morlock, you must return to Paragraph 1 and redo your adventure from the beginning.

rows.jp: なんか昔読んだ本と思考がまざったことをお詫びするよ。
rows.en: I apologize for letting my thoughts get mixed up with some book I read long ago.

ghs.en: I apologize for getting a book I read a long time ago mingled with my thoughts.

rows.jp: やっぱ無理があった。一人は。
rows.en: I could not pull it off after all. Not alone.

ghs.en: I knew it, it's impossible. Being alone I mean.

rows.jp: ここで曜子特派員にカメラを！
rows.en: And now, camera to our correspondent Yoko!

ghs.en: Let us turn our camera to Special Correspondent Youko!

rows.jp: おおっと、いました！
rows.en: Oh! There she is!

ghs.en: Ohmmmy, she was here!
ghs.assessment: おおっと marks a mock-presenter's sudden discovery: 'whoa, there she is.' The English invents a stretched 'oh my' and changes immediate sight into a past statement.
ghs.remedy: Whoa, there she is!

rows.jp: ばっちり見られちゃってるるる！
rows.en: She can see me perfectly-ly-ly!

ghs.en: She has totally seen me-eh-eh!

rows.jp: さすが正式な訓練を受けた市原です。
rows.en: Just what you would expect from the formally trained Ichihara.

ghs.en: Naught else may be expected from one who received formal Ichihara training.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese attributes the feat to formally trained Ichihara herself. The English turns her family name into a type or school of training that some unnamed person received.
ghs.remedy: Just what you'd expect from the formally trained Ichihara.

highlights.text: one who received formal Ichihara training

rows.jp: 違います。
rows.en: No, that is not it.

ghs.en: That is incorrect.

rows.jp: だいぶ異なものです。
rows.en: She is something far stranger.

ghs.en: That is considerably unusual.

rows.jp: 異質です。
rows.en: An anomaly.

ghs.en: It is heterogeneous.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that she is qualitatively alien or different from ordinary people. 'Heterogeneous' is a technical property of a mixture and is not an idiomatic description of a person.
ghs.remedy: She's fundamentally different.

rows.jp: えーと、ごっつ優秀すぎるって感じで異質です。
rows.en: Uh—an anomaly in the sense that she is way too absurdly capable.

ghs.en: Uhmmm, it is heterogeneous due to feeling like extra-super competent.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese explains that her difference lies in being far too extraordinarily capable. The English retains the inapplicable technical adjective and uses a malformed causal phrase ending in 'competent.'
ghs.remedy: She's different because she is simply far too capable.

highlights.text: heterogeneous due to feeling like extra-super competent

rows.jp: 失敗がない人間って、どうなんでしょう？
rows.en: What do we make of someone who never fails?

ghs.en: What does one do about humans that have no failings?
ghs.assessment: Taichi wonders what one should make of a person who never fails. The English instead asks what action should be taken regarding multiple humans without character flaws.
ghs.remedy: What are we supposed to make of someone who never fails?

highlights.text: What does one do about humans that have no failings?

rows.jp: 失敗する率が極端に低い人間って、言葉にするとそれだけですが。
rows.en: Put it into words, and all you have is someone with an extremely low failure rate.

ghs.en: Well, once it has been put into words, it is merely a human with an extremely low probability of failure.

rows.jp: 普通の人が百回死ぬような事態に二百回生存しちゃうげな。
rows.en: Someone who survives two hundred situations that would kill an ordinary person a hundred times over, and such.

ghs.en: Like in a situation where a normal person would die a hundred times, they'd survive two hundred times.

rows.jp: そりゃほとんどアータ！　ホーリーウッドの一時間四十五分時点の主人公の性能ですよ。
rows.en: Why, those are practically the stats of a Holywood protagonist at the one-hour-forty-five-minute mark!

ghs.en: That is almost like an ah'tress! That is the performance of a Holywood protagonist at the one hour, forty-five minutes mark!
ghs.assessment: The Japanese mock address アータ is not 'actress,' while the following reference is to a Hollywood protagonist. The English invents an eye-dialect occupation and misspells Hollywood.
ghs.remedy: Why, that's practically the performance of a Hollywood protagonist

rows.jp: ラスト十分前が一番性能が高いわけですな。
rows.en: Those last ten minutes are when they hit peak performance.

ghs.en: Before the last ten minutes, their performances are at the absolute highest, indeed.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that a protagonist's abilities peak during the ten minutes before the ending. The English says they peak before that final ten-minute interval begins.
ghs.remedy: In the final ten minutes

rows.jp: そこで考えた、アンチ映画。
rows.en: So I devised the anti-movie.

ghs.en: And with that I thought: anti-movie.

rows.jp: ラスト十分まで昼寝しまくって、最後に超人モードになって敵を倒すストーリー。
rows.en: A story where the hero naps nonstop until the final ten minutes, switches into superhuman mode, and defeats the enemy.

ghs.en: A story where until the last ten minutes he does nothing but take naps, then at the end he goes into Hyperman Mode and defeats the bad guy.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that the hero enters a generic superhuman mode. The English invents and capitalizes the proper transformation name 'Hyperman Mode.'
ghs.remedy: superhuman mode

rows.jp: あとまったく脈絡なくもう一つ考えた。
rows.en: I also had another completely unrelated idea.

ghs.en: And then without a damn trace of logical connection I had one more idea:
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that the next idea has absolutely no logical connection, without adding a curse.
ghs.remedy: without any logical connection whatsoever

rows.jp: 人類滅亡からはじまるストーリー。
rows.en: A story that begins with the extinction of humanity.

ghs.en: a story that has its beginning with the Fall of Mankind.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese plainly says that the story begins with humanity's extinction. The English substitutes a capitalized, euphemistic phrase that can mean moral decline rather than annihilation.
ghs.remedy: the extinction of humanity

rows.jp: これやん。
rows.en: This is it.

ghs.en: That, yah.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese colloquial exclamation means 'This is it' or 'that's the one.' The English produces an incomplete deictic fragment with an unsupported dialect spelling.
ghs.remedy: This is it.

rows.jp: まさに俺って感じだ。
rows.en: It feels exactly like me.

ghs.en: Really feels me-ish.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that the idea feels exactly like Taichi. The English omits the subject and creates the awkward adjective 'me-ish.'
ghs.remedy: That feels exactly like me.

rows.jp: 自分賛美歌。
rows.en: A hymn to myself.

ghs.en: It's a hymn to the self.

rows.jp: 人を貶めることで自分を高める行為とどっちが卑しいだろう？
rows.en: Which is baser: singing my own praises, or putting other people down to raise myself up?

ghs.en: But which is vulgar now, that or making oneself great by tearing down others?

rows.jp: そこいらどうなんだろう？
rows.en: How does that one shake out?

ghs.en: Well, what do we do about that?
ghs.assessment: Taichi wonders how that moral comparison should be judged. The English asks what practical action should be taken.
ghs.remedy: I wonder how that balance works out.

highlights.text: what do we do about that?

rows.jp: 俺は問いかけた。
rows.en: I asked.

ghs.en: I asked out.
ghs.assessment: 問いかける means that Taichi posed the question. 'Asked out' means inviting someone on a date and lacks an object here.
ghs.remedy: I posed the question.

rows.jp: 「ブライダルお姫様だっこ」
rows.en: “Bridal princess carry.”

ghs.en: Youko: "Bridal princess carry."

rows.jp: すっげ哲学的。まいった。勝てない。
rows.en: That's insanely philosophical. You got me. I can't top that.

ghs.en: Waaay philosophical. Bummer. I can't beat this.
ghs.assessment: まいった here means that the answer has defeated or outdone him. 'Bummer' instead labels the situation disappointing.
ghs.remedy: You got me.

rows.jp: もうっ、カメラ返せよ！
rows.en: Hey! Give me back the camera already!

ghs.en: Awww, give me my camera back now!

rows.jp: 誰と遊ぼう？
rows.en: Who should I play with?

ghs.en: Who do I play with?

rows.jp: じゃ、みみ先輩だ。
rows.en: Then Mimi it is.

ghs.en: Yeah, Mimi-senpai.

rows.jp: 寝てるよ！
rows.en: She's asleep!

ghs.en: She's asleep!

rows.jp: 起きたあっ！？
rows.en: She woke up?!

ghs.en: She woke uuup?!

rows.jp: 「モラルの欠如、行きすぎた利己的な個人主義、自分が怠惰に過ごすために利用される基本的人権、このようないい子ハザードによって汚染されている現代社会に――」
rows.en: “A lack of morals, runaway selfish individualism, fundamental human rights invoked as excuses for personal idleness—modern society stands contaminated by this Good-Kid Hazard――”

rows.jp: 「私たち若者は互いに築き上げる交友を持つことができるのでしょうか？　我が群青学院放送部は、この疑問に対して満足のゆく答えを提供することができると考えています」
rows.en: “Can young people like us still build meaningful bonds with one another? The Gunjo Academy Broadcasting Club believes it can provide a satisfactory answer to this question.”

rows.jp: うへえ！
rows.en: Yikes!

ghs.en: Uweeeh!

rows.jp: 大きく出たな。
rows.en: That's quite a claim.

ghs.en: A big one came out!
ghs.assessment: 大きく出た means that Misato made an audacious or grand claim. The English literalizes size and emergence as a large object coming out.
ghs.remedy: That's a bold claim!

rows.jp: さすがみみみ先輩。
rows.en: That's Mimimi for you.

ghs.en: What else from Mimimi-senpai.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese means 'just what you'd expect from Mimimi-senpai.' The English omits the verb and uses an opaque rhetorical fragment.
ghs.remedy: Just what you'd expect from Mimimi-senpai.

rows.jp: この人の弱さってのは、なんかおっぱいの感触と似てる。
rows.en: There's something about her vulnerability that's like the feel of a breast.

ghs.en: The weakness of this person sort of resembles the tactile sensation of boobs.

rows.jp: だから大好きというのが本音だ。
rows.en: Truth is, that's why I love her.

ghs.en: Therefore great love is the true intent here.
ghs.assessment: Taichi says frankly that this is why he loves her. The English turns his feeling into the abstract subject 'great love' and his candid admission into an unspecified intent.
ghs.remedy: That's why I love her, honestly.

highlights.text: Therefore great love is the true intent here.

rows.jp: 実は好きでも何でもない。
rows.en: Actually, I don't like her at all.

ghs.en: Truth is, love's sorta whatever.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese bluntly retracts the claim: in truth, he does not like her at all. The English instead expresses vague indifference toward love as a concept.
ghs.remedy: Actually, I don't like her at all.

rows.jp: 好きになるって設定上で定めただけだ。
rows.en: I only made falling for her part of the setup.

ghs.en: That we'd fall in love is just something established by the scenario's Settei.
ghs.assessment: Taichi says only that the setting defines him as liking her. The English makes the love mutual, invents a scenario as possessor, and leaves 設定 as an unexplained capitalized loanword.
ghs.remedy: The setting merely says that I'm supposed to like her.

rows.jp: ごめんなさい。
rows.en: Sorry.

ghs.en: Apologies.

rows.jp: やさぐれちゃったよ！！
rows.en: Now you've gone all sullen!!

ghs.en: She's sulking now!!!
ghs.assessment: The Japanese first-person comic outburst says that Taichi himself has become sullen or cynical. The English assigns the state to a woman.
ghs.remedy: Now I'm getting bitter!

rows.jp: そんなに『みみみ』呼ばわりはイヤなのかよ！
rows.en: You hate being called “Mimimi” that much?!

ghs.en: Is that how much she hates to be called "Mimimi"?!

rows.jp: 超可愛いのになぁ。
rows.en: It's so cute, though.

ghs.en: C'mon, but it's Hyper Kawaii...
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says in colloquial Japanese that the nickname is extremely cute. The English mixes an English intensifier with an unexplained Japanese adjective and capitalizes both.
ghs.remedy: super cute

rows.jp: ちぇっ。
rows.en: Tch.

ghs.en: Tsk.

rows.jp: とすると美希だな。
rows.en: Then Miki it is.

ghs.en: Let's follow that up with Miki then.

rows.jp: 慰めてもらうしか。
rows.en: I'll just have to get her to comfort me.

ghs.en: I get nothing but consolation.
ghs.assessment: Taichi decides that he has no choice but to seek comfort from Miki. The English states that consolation is already the only thing he receives.
ghs.remedy: I'll have to get Miki to comfort me.

rows.jp: ぉぃぉぃ！
rows.en: hey, hey!

ghs.en: (hey now!)

rows.jp: おいおい！
rows.en: Hey, hey!

ghs.en: HEY NOW!

rows.jp: 多重放送になった俺だ。
rows.en: There I am, a multiplex broadcast.

ghs.en: I ended up as a multiplex broadcast.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese jokes that Taichi's repeated internal voices have become a layered or multiple broadcast. The English says that Taichi himself literally became the broadcast medium.
ghs.remedy: My voice turned into a multiplex broadcast.

highlights.text: I ended up as a multiplex broadcast.

rows.jp: モノローグでだけどな。
rows.en: Only in my monologue, though.

ghs.en: Only via monologue, though.

rows.jp: しっかし、すげえサービス精神旺盛な成果物だな。
rows.en: Still, talk about a product that's eager to please.

ghs.en: Annnd yet, that's one finished delivered product that's chock full of that waaay amazing Service spirit!
ghs.assessment: The Japanese calls the work a product overflowing with eagerness to entertain or please. The English stacks redundant production adjectives and capitalizes an awkward calque as though it were a named doctrine.
ghs.remedy: That's one work packed with an incredible eagerness to please.

rows.jp: いいのか？
rows.en: Is that okay?

ghs.en: Is that OK?

rows.jp: 許されるのか？
rows.en: Is it allowed?

ghs.en: Will that be permitted?

rows.jp: 認証されたのか？
rows.en: Has it been certified?

ghs.en: Will it pass certification?

rows.jp: アダルト・カテゴリに入れるのか？
rows.en: Can it go in the adult category?

ghs.en: Will it be put in the Adults category?
ghs.assessment: The Japanese refers to the singular adult category. The English uses the plural personal noun 'Adults' as an attributive category name.
ghs.remedy: adult category

rows.jp: 「ごろにゃーごろ」
rows.en: “Purrow-meowrr.”

ghs.en: Miki: "Purr-meow-purr."

rows.jp: 猫語か！
rows.en: That's cat language!

ghs.en: Catspeak?!

rows.jp: まいったな、履修してないぞ。
rows.en: Damn. I never took that course.

ghs.en: I give up, I didn't study that.

rows.jp: 意思の疎通ができない。
rows.en: We can't communicate.

ghs.en: Reciprocal understanding of intent is impossible.

rows.en: At this rate, I'll become a man who does nothing but stare at underwear.

ghs.en: It seems I ended up as someone who just looks at panties.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that at this rate Taichi is liable to become such a person. The English says that the transformation already happened and only now appears evident.
ghs.remedy: It looks as though I'll become

rows.jp: よしなろう。
rows.en: All right. I'll become one.

ghs.en: That'd be good thing to be.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese is Taichi's immediate resolution: 'All right, I'll become one.' The English turns it into a hypothetical evaluation and omits the article before 'good thing.'
ghs.remedy: All right, I'll become one.

highlights.text: That'd be good thing to be.

rows.jp: 俺はおよそ十四時間、下着を凝視した。
rows.en: I stared at the underwear for about fourteen hours.

ghs.en: And I, for roughly fourteen hours, fixed a stare on the underwear.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that he stared fixedly at the underwear. The English calques the act into the nonidiomatic collocation 'fix a stare on.'
ghs.remedy: stared fixedly at the underwear

highlights.text: fixed a stare on the underwear

rows.jp: 時間にして四秒ほどの出来事だった。
rows.en: That all happened in about four seconds.

ghs.en: As far as time is concerned it was an event about four seconds long.

rows.jp: ありがとう美希。
rows.en: Thanks, Miki.

ghs.en: Thank you, Miki.

rows.jp: グンナイ。
rows.en: G'night.

ghs.en: GUNAI (good night).
ghs.assessment: The source gives only the stylized phonetic form グンナイ. The English appends an explanatory parenthesis rather than allowing the stylization to function directly.
ghs.remedy: G'night.

rows.jp: 遊びのあとはレクリエーション。
rows.en: After playtime comes recreation.

ghs.en: After playing around we have recreation.

rows.jp: 部活に精を出す。
rows.en: I throw myself into club activities.

ghs.en: I spurt forth my spirit in the club.
ghs.assessment: 精を出す is an idiom meaning to apply oneself diligently. The English turns effort into a bodily emission of spirit and adds sexualized physical imagery.
ghs.remedy: I throw myself into club work.

highlights.text: I spurt forth my spirit in the club.

rows.jp: エッチラオッチラ。
rows.en: Heave-ho, heave-ho.

ghs.en: Laboriously with a lot of sexfort.
ghs.assessment: エッチラオッチラ is a fixed comic description of laborious effort. The English invents a sex pun and the nonexistent blend 'sexfort.'
ghs.remedy: Heave-ho, heave-ho.

rows.jp: 自動的に働く。
rows.en: I work automatically.

ghs.en: Working automatically.

rows.jp: 人は誰だってなかば自動的なんだ。
rows.en: Everyone's half automatic.

ghs.en: People, all of them, are semi-automatic.

rows.jp: それの、どこが悪い？
rows.en: What's wrong with that?

ghs.en: And what part of that, exactly, is bad?

rows.jp: 「退屈で、気が狂いそうになりますよ？」
rows.en: “But I would be so bored I would lose my mind, you know?”

ghs.en: Miki: "I would just lose my mind from boredom, wouldn't I?"

rows.jp: え？
rows.en: Huh?

ghs.en: Eh?

rows.jp: 「あ、だめ、だめですよっ！？」
rows.en: “No! Don’t! You can’t!”

ghs.en: Yusa: "Ah, you can't, you can't do that!"

rows.jp: だめって、何が？
rows.en: What do you mean, I can't?

ghs.en: Can't, what exactly?
ghs.assessment: Taichi asks what exactly is forbidden. The English copies Japanese ellipsis and word order into an unnatural question.
ghs.remedy: What exactly can't I do?

rows.jp: 空。
rows.en: Sky.

ghs.en: The sky,

rows.jp: そして。
rows.en: And—

ghs.en: and then,

rows.jp: 地面。遙か下方。
rows.en: The ground. Far below.

ghs.en: the ground. Far, far below.

rows.jp: その瞬間。
rows.en: At that instant.

ghs.en: That instant,

rows.jp: 破裂―――
rows.en: Rupture―――

ghs.en: rupture---

rows.jp: 「あああああああああああああああああああああああああああああああああああああああああああああああああああっ！！！！」
rows.en: “Aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaah!!!!”

ghs.en: Taichi: "AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAH!!!!!"

rows.jp: 語句の連結が外れてできた言葉の海から、俺は手を伸ばす。
rows.en: From a sea of words formed when the links between phrases came undone, I reach out.

ghs.en: I stretch my hand out from the ocean of words that had managed to undo the connection with sentences.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese describes a sea of words formed when the connections among phrases came apart. The English makes words intentionally succeed at severing a connection they had 'with sentences' and does not identify the relations among the words themselves.
ghs.remedy: the sea of words left when the links between phrases came apart

highlights.text: words that had managed to undo the connection with sentences

rows.jp: 掴む藁もない。
rows.en: There's no straw to clutch at.

ghs.en: I grasp no straw.

rows.jp: くるりと意識を反転して（たこ焼きのように）現世に戻る。
rows.en: I flip my consciousness over (like a takoyaki) and return to the present world.

ghs.en: Suddenly spinning and covering myself in consciousness (like a takoyaki) I return to the present world.
ghs.assessment: Taichi flips his consciousness around like turning a takoyaki and returns to the present world. The English instead makes him spin bodily and wrap himself in consciousness.
ghs.remedy: I flip my consciousness over (like a takoyaki) and return to the present world.

highlights.text: spinning and covering myself in consciousness

rows.jp: 意識が現世を観測してのけた。
rows.en: My consciousness manages to observe the present world.

ghs.en: Consciousness wrung to observing the present world.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that his consciousness successfully managed to observe the present world. The English uses 'wrung' without a coherent object or construction.
ghs.remedy: My consciousness managed to observe the present world.

highlights.text: Consciousness wrung to observing the present world.

rows.jp: 「はっ、はっ、はっ……」
rows.en: “Hah, hah, hah...”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Hah, hah, hah..."

rows.jp: 俺は、自ら破壊したフェンスから身を乗り出そうとしていた。
rows.en: I was trying to lean out through the opening I'd torn in the fence myself.

ghs.en: I had just about begun to lean myself out of the fence that I had wrecked by myself.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that he was about to lean his body out through the opening in the fence. The English uses the transitive reflexive 'lean myself' and treats the fence as a container he is emerging from.
ghs.remedy: lean out through the opening in the fence

highlights.text: lean myself out of the fence

rows.jp: 強ばった指が、左右の金網をつかんでいる。
rows.en: My stiffened fingers grip the wire mesh on either side.

ghs.en: Stiffened fingers are grasping the wire mesh on the left and right.

rows.jp: ギリギリのところだったのだろう。
rows.en: I must have been right on the brink.

ghs.en: This was just barely the last moment indeed.

rows.jp: フェンスは扉大にくりぬかれていた。
rows.en: A doorway-sized section had been cut out of the fence.

ghs.en: The fence had been excavated into door size.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that a door-sized opening had been cut out of the fence. 'Excavated' refers to digging earth or removing buried material, and 'into door size' is ungrammatical.
ghs.remedy: A door-sized opening had been cut out of the fence.

rows.jp: 俺がやった。その記憶がある。
rows.en: I did it. I remember that.

ghs.en: My doing. I have the recollections of that.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese gives two direct assertions: he did it, and he remembers doing it. The English creates a possessive noun fragment and pluralizes memory into formal 'recollections.'
ghs.remedy: I did it. I remember.

highlights.text: My doing. I have the recollections of that.

rows.jp: 記憶するはしからズタズタに分断され、他の言語に混じって判断できなくなっていたんだ。
rows.en: Each memory was torn to pieces the moment I recalled it, mixed among other languages until I could no longer make sense of anything.

ghs.en: No sooner than they had been memorized they had been torn up into tiny pieces and mixed with other languages, that I could no longer decipher them.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that memories were shredded even as he formed them and mixed with other language until he could no longer judge them. The English changes remembering into deliberate memorization, pluralizes 'language,' and joins the result with an ungrammatical 'that.'
ghs.remedy: As soon as I formed a memory, it was torn apart and mixed with other language until I could no longer make sense of it.

highlights.text: No sooner than they had been memorized

rows.jp: 指先が石膏のように白い。
rows.en: My fingertips are white as plaster.

ghs.en: My fingertips are as white as plaster.

rows.jp: ずっと力んでいたせいか。
rows.en: Maybe from straining for so long?

ghs.en: Perhaps because they have been gripping all along.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese attributes the pallor to prolonged straining or tension. The English narrows that cause to the fingertips themselves continuously performing the act of gripping.
ghs.remedy: Maybe because I had been straining so hard.

highlights.text: because they have been gripping all along

rows.jp: 重心を背後に引き戻した。
rows.en: I shift my weight back.

ghs.en: I restore my center of gravity to my back.
ghs.assessment: Taichi shifts his center of gravity backward to regain safety. The English treats his back as a location to which the center of gravity belongs or returns.
ghs.remedy: I shift my center of gravity backward.

highlights.text: restore my center of gravity to my back

rows.jp: これで安全。落ちない。
rows.en: Safe now. I won't fall.

ghs.en: This is safe. I won't fall.

rows.jp: なおフェンスに食い込んでいる指。苦労してはがす。
rows.en: My fingers are still biting into the fence. I struggle to peel them away.

ghs.en: Still the fingertips eat down into the fence. I peel off with difficulty.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that his fingers are still digging into the fence and that he painfully peels them away. The English personifies the fingertips as eating downward and omits the object of 'peel off.'
ghs.remedy: My fingers are still dug into the fence. I struggle to peel them away.

highlights.text: the fingertips eat down into the fence. I peel off

rows.jp: 軽い苦痛。
rows.en: A twinge of pain.

ghs.en: Mild pain.

rows.jp: 裏返すと、うっすらと網目状に血が浮いていた。
rows.en: I turn my hands over. Faint traces of blood show in a mesh pattern.

ghs.en: When I turn them upside down, blood was surfacing in a reticulate.
ghs.assessment: When he turns his hands over, faint blood rises in a mesh pattern. The English shifts tense, uses the adjective 'reticulate' as an incomplete count noun, and omits the pattern's visible form.
ghs.remedy: faint blood had risen in a mesh pattern

highlights.text: blood was surfacing in a reticulate

ghs.en: Taichi: "I...
ghs.assessment: The English dialogue opens a quotation mark but never closes it.
ghs.remedy: Taichi: "I..."

rows.jp: 自殺しようとしたことが、信じられない。
rows.en: I can't believe I tried to kill myself.

ghs.en: I can't believe it, I was trying to commit suicide.
ghs.assessment: The English joins two independent clauses with a comma and makes 'it' an unexplained object before restating the actual fact.
ghs.remedy: I can't believe I was trying

highlights.text: I can't believe it, I was trying

rows.jp: 死んではいけない。
rows.en: I mustn't die.

ghs.en: Death is out of the question.

rows.jp: たくさん殺して、生きたのだから。
rows.en: Because I killed so many people and lived.

ghs.en: Because you made a living by killing so much.
ghs.assessment: Taichi tells himself that he killed many and nevertheless lived, which is why he must not die now. The English shifts to second person and turns survival after killing into earning a livelihood through killing.
ghs.remedy: Because I've killed so many and survived.

highlights.text: you made a living by killing so much

rows.jp: 「そうなんだろ……曜子ちゃん？」
rows.en: “That's right……isn't it, Yoko?”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Isn't that right... Youko-chan?"

rows.jp: 呼んでも、彼女はあらわれない。
rows.en: I call out, but she doesn't appear.

ghs.en: I call her, but the girl does not turn up.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese uses the established pronoun 'she.' Calling her 'the girl' introduces detached narrator language at an intimate moment.
ghs.remedy: she

rows.jp: 自分を抱きしめる。
rows.en: I wrap my arms around myself.

ghs.en: I hug myself.

rows.jp: 寒い。
rows.en: Cold.

ghs.en: So cold.

rows.jp: いてもたってもいられなくなる。
rows.en: I can't stay still.

ghs.en: I become unable to sit still.

rows.jp: 走り出す。
rows.en: I break into a run.

ghs.en: I start to run.

rows.jp: 校内に。
rows.en: Into the school.

ghs.en: Inside the school building.

rows.jp: 「うわあああああああああああああっ」
rows.en: “Aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaah!”

ghs.en: Taichi: "WAAAAAAAAAAAAAAH!"

rows.jp: 駆ける。
rows.en: I run.

ghs.en: I dash.

rows.jp: 人！
rows.en: People!

ghs.en: People!

rows.jp: 人！
rows.en: People!

ghs.en: People!

rows.jp: どっかに人！
rows.en: Someone—anywhere!

ghs.en: Anywhere, people!
ghs.assessment: Taichi desperately calls for any person to be somewhere. The English reverses the order into an ungrammatical location-plus-plural fragment.
ghs.remedy: Someone! Anywhere!

rows.jp: 「美希、霧！」
rows.en: “Miki! Kiri!”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Miki, Kiri!"

rows.jp: いない。
rows.en: No one.

ghs.en: Not here.

rows.jp: 机を倒していく。
rows.en: I knock over desks as I go.

ghs.en: I throw around the desks.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says that he knocks desks over as he proceeds. 'Throw around' suggests lifting and hurling them in multiple directions.
ghs.remedy: knock over the desks

rows.jp: どんどん倒していく。
rows.en: I knock them down, one after another.

ghs.en: Knock them down one after the other.
ghs.assessment: The surrounding first-person narration requires an explicit subject in this English sentence.
ghs.remedy: I knock them down

rows.jp: 教科書が床に滑り落ちる。
rows.en: Textbooks slide to the floor.

ghs.en: Textbooks slip down to the ground.
ghs.assessment: The textbooks slide onto the interior floor. 'Ground' normally denotes outdoor earth or terrain.
ghs.remedy: to the floor

rows.jp: 二人はいない。
rows.en: Neither of them is there.

ghs.en: The two are not among us.

ghs.remedy: Neither of them is here.

highlights.text: The two are not among us.

rows.jp: 恐怖。
rows.en: Fear.

ghs.en: Terror.

rows.jp: この空間には誰もいない。
rows.en: There is no one in this space.

ghs.en: In this room there is no one.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese expands the realization to this entire space, not merely the current room. The English narrows the absence to one room.
ghs.remedy: In this whole space

rows.jp: 逃げ出す。
rows.en: I flee.

ghs.en: I run away.

rows.jp: 長細い空間。
rows.en: A long, narrow space.

ghs.en: A thin and narrow space.
ghs.assessment: 長細い describes a long, narrow space. The English replaces length with thinness and then redundantly adds narrowness.
ghs.remedy: A long, narrow space.

rows.jp: 挟み撃ちにされたら助からないという危機感。
rows.en: The fear that if I'm caught in a pincer here, I won't survive.

ghs.en: A sense of impeding danger that says I would never survive should I be subjected to a pincer attack.
ghs.assessment: The intended word is 'impending,' not 'impeding,' and the internal warning does not literally speak a proposition.
ghs.remedy: impending danger: I would never survive

rows.jp: 敵は虚無だ。
rows.en: The enemy is nothingness.
